items.followUp: State two differences between Rutherford’s and Bohr’s atomic models.

rubric.why: Identifies the central nucleus and the motion of electrons in Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Rutherford’s model has a small central nucleus with electrons revolving around it.
rubric.how: Award for both the nucleus and revolving electrons.

rubric.why: Distinguishes Rutherford’s model from Bohr’s fixed energy levels.
rubric.description: Rutherford did not specify fixed energy levels or orbits for electrons.
rubric.how: Award for stating that fixed energy levels or orbits were absent.

rubric.why: States Bohr’s key addition to the atomic model.
rubric.description: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy specific fixed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for fixed orbits or energy levels.

rubric.why: Explains how Bohr accounted for atomic stability and changes in electron energy.
rubric.description: Electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy; they absorb or emit energy when changing levels.
rubric.how: Award for either the no-radiation explanation or energy changes during transitions.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus, with electrons revolving around it.
Rutherford’s model did not describe fixed energy levels for the electrons and could not explain the stability of the atom.
Bohr proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in specific fixed orbits, each having a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while in these stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when they move between energy levels.

items.followUp: Differentiate between polar and non-polar covalent bonds, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Identifies unequal sharing of electrons in a polar covalent bond.
rubric.description: A polar covalent bond forms when the bonded atoms share electrons unequally.
rubric.how: Award for stating that sharing is unequal.

rubric.why: Recognises the separation of charge in a polar bond and gives an acceptable example.
rubric.description: Unequal sharing produces partial positive and negative ends; HCl or H₂O is an example.
rubric.how: Award for polarity/partial charges with an example such as HCl or H₂O.

rubric.why: Identifies equal sharing of electrons in a non-polar covalent bond.
rubric.description: A non-polar covalent bond forms when bonded atoms share electrons equally.
rubric.how: Award for stating that sharing is equal.

rubric.why: Recognises the absence of charged ends and gives an acceptable example.
rubric.description: A non-polar bond has no charged ends; H₂, Cl₂ or O₂ is an example.
rubric.how: Award for absence of poles/partial charges with an example such as H₂, Cl₂ or O₂.

modelAnswer: In a polar covalent bond, the bonded atoms share the electron pair unequally, so partial positive and negative ends develop; HCl is an example.
In a non-polar covalent bond, the bonded atoms share the electron pair equally, so no poles develop; Cl₂ is an example.

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and explain how temperature and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Includes the essential conditions in the definition of vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by vapour in equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature.
rubric.how: Award for pressure by vapour in equilibrium with the liquid.

rubric.why: States the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Increasing temperature increases vapour pressure because more liquid particles escape into the vapour.
rubric.how: Award for the correct direction of change and a valid explanation.

rubric.why: Connects weaker intermolecular attraction with greater evaporation and vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Liquids with weaker intermolecular forces generally have higher vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for the correct relationship between weaker forces and higher pressure.

rubric.why: States the contrasting effect of stronger intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Stronger intermolecular forces hold particles in the liquid, giving a lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for the correct relationship between stronger forces and lower pressure.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of a non-volatile dissolved substance, another textbook factor.
rubric.description: A non-volatile solute or impurity lowers the vapour pressure of a liquid.
rubric.how: Award for correctly stating that a non-volatile solute/impurity lowers vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapours of a liquid when they are in equilibrium with the liquid at a particular temperature.
Temperature: On increasing temperature, more liquid particles gain enough energy to escape into the vapour phase, so vapour pressure increases.
Nature of the liquid: Liquids with weaker intermolecular forces evaporate more readily and have higher vapour pressure; stronger forces give lower vapour pressure.
Non-volatile solute: Dissolving a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid.

items.followUp: Name and briefly explain four physical properties of metals.

rubric.why: Recognises malleability as a characteristic physical property.
rubric.description: Metals can be hammered into thin sheets (malleability).
rubric.how: Award for malleability or the ability to form sheets.

rubric.why: Recognises ductility as a characteristic physical property.
rubric.description: Metals can be drawn into wires (ductility).
rubric.how: Award for ductility or the ability to form wires.

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic lustre of metals.
rubric.description: Metals generally have a shiny surface or metallic lustre.
rubric.how: Award for lustre or shininess.

rubric.why: Identifies metals’ ability to conduct heat or electricity.
rubric.description: Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity.
rubric.how: Award for correctly naming either or both forms of conductivity.

rubric.why: Identifies sonority as another physical property of metals.
rubric.description: Metals produce a ringing sound when struck (sonority).
rubric.how: Award for sonority or the ringing sound when struck.

modelAnswer: Metals are malleable: they can be hammered into thin sheets.
Metals are ductile: they can be drawn into wires.
Metals are lustrous and generally have a shiny surface.
Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity.
Metals are sonorous: they produce a ringing sound when struck.

items.followUp: Define organic chemistry and inorganic chemistry.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of physical chemistry.
rubric.description: Physical chemistry studies the physical properties and behaviour of matter and the energy changes associated with them.
rubric.how: Award for defining physical chemistry in terms of physical properties/behaviour or energy changes.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of nuclear chemistry.
rubric.description: Nuclear chemistry studies changes that take place in the nuclei of atoms and the associated nuclear reactions.
rubric.how: Award for identifying chemistry concerned with atomic nuclei or nuclear reactions.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the physical properties and behaviour of matter and the energy changes involved in chemical processes.
Nuclear chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with changes in the nuclei of atoms and the nuclear reactions associated with them.

items.followUp: Name four gases found in air and state which is present in the greatest amount.

rubric.why: Checks that the student can name gases that occur in air.
rubric.description: Names any two gases present in air.
rubric.how: Award for any two correct gases from air.

rubric.why: Checks for two additional correct examples to make four.
rubric.description: Names two further gases present in air, giving four names in total.
rubric.how: Award for two additional correct gases from air.

modelAnswer: Nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide are four gases present in air.
Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in air.

items.followUp: Describe the observations in Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment and what they showed about the atom.

rubric.why: Identifies the experimental evidence used to study the distribution of mass in an atom.
rubric.description: Rutherford directed alpha particles at a very thin gold foil.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the alpha-particle experiment, preferably with the gold foil.

rubric.why: Uses the scattering observations to support the conclusion about the atom’s centre.
rubric.description: Most alpha particles passed through, but a few were strongly deflected or bounced back, showing that nearly all the atom’s mass is concentrated in a small, dense nucleus.
rubric.how: Award for the observation that most passed through and the conclusion that mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

modelAnswer: Rutherford bombarded a thin gold foil with fast-moving alpha particles.
Most alpha particles passed straight through, but a very small number were strongly deflected or bounced back.
The results showed that almost the whole mass of the atom is concentrated in a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre.

items.followUp: What are cathode rays? How are they produced in a discharge tube?

rubric.why: Explains how the gas in the tube forms positive ions.
rubric.description: Fast electrons in the discharge tube collide with gas atoms or molecules and knock out electrons, forming positive ions.
rubric.how: Award for ionisation of the gas by electron collisions.

rubric.why: Explains how the positive ions form the observed anode (canal) rays.
rubric.description: The positive ions move towards the cathode and pass through its holes, forming anode rays (canal rays).
rubric.how: Award for positive ions passing through the perforated cathode and forming anode/canal rays.

modelAnswer: In a discharge tube, fast-moving electrons collide with atoms or molecules of the gas and remove electrons from them, producing positive ions.
These positive ions are attracted towards the cathode; some pass through the holes in the cathode and form anode rays, also called canal rays.
